slides.text: Court stenographers don't hear words; we hear phonetic chords. After fifteen years of typing two hundred and twenty words a minute, my fingers move on pure subconscious reflex whenever someone speaks in a room. Tonight, during a closed-door deposition on the fiftieth floor, the backup generators failed, plunging the boardroom into pitch darkness for four minutes.

Nobody spoke a word in the dark—or so I thought. When the lights flickered back on, the defense attorney was dead in his leather chair from an apparent heart attack, and everyone else was still seated ten feet away. The police ruled it natural causes on the spot. It wasn't until I got home at midnight that I unspooled the paper phonetic tape from my stenotype machine.

During those four minutes of total silence, my fingers had unconsciously transcribed a whispered conversation too faint for my conscious ears to register. Two voices had spoken right beside my chair. One was the dead lawyer begging for his life. The other voice—the one calmly explaining how potassium chloride mimics cardiac arrest—had dictated a phonetic cadence I knew by heart: my husband's stutter.
